chapter_title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Building Equilateral Triangles with Compass and Ruler

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles (diagram given with one circle).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150
homework.description: Use points on two (or three) equal circles and/or their centres A, B (and C) to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: can a marked ruler alone build an equilateral triangle? Students attempt a quick freehand sketch and note the difficulty of ensuring all three sides are equal. Collect observations to motivate the compass-and-arc method.

Demonstrate the three-step arc method on the board: draw base AB of 4 cm, swing an arc of radius 4 cm from A, swing a second arc of radius 4 cm from B, mark C at their intersection, then join AC and BC. Ask students to explain why C lies on both arcs, establishing that AC = BC = 4 cm.

Students work through Construct, section 7.1 p.150 ("Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm)...") for parts (a)–(e), then attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150 ("Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles..."). Circulate to check arc placement and pencil pressure.

Students share one completed construction under the visualiser or on the board. Class identifies which constructions produced equilateral triangles and articulates the shared arc-radius property that guarantees all sides equal.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently swing arcs with inconsistent compass width between the two centre points — insist they set and lock the compass radius before each arc. Watch for students who join endpoints before checking that both arcs have been drawn from the correct centre. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150 ("Use points on two or three equal circles...") makes a useful self-study extension for students who finish quickly.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: When Do Three Lengths Make a Triangle?

textbook_items_in_class.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles? Explain using the triangle inequality.

For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'? Explore. Also find which length can be identified as immediately less than the sum without calculation.

time_bands.activity: Pairs attempt Math Talk, section 7.2 p.151 ("Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm...") with compass and ruler. Students describe what they observe — the arcs fail to meet — and record their finding.

Introduce the tent-tree-pole path metaphor from the prose: a direct path between two points is always shorter than a detour through a third. Groups generate additional impossible length sets and look for the common condition. Bring findings together: each side must be less than the sum of the other two.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154 ("Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles?...") and Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.154 ("For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy..."). The second item pushes them to notice that only the largest side needs checking.

Class discussion: students articulate the triangle inequality as a decision rule in their own words. Invite one student to show which single comparison is sufficient when the largest side is identified, and why.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight — that only the largest side needs to be compared with the sum of the other two — often elude students who apply all three comparisons mechanically; build toward it through Try This Q3 rather than stating it outright. Watch for students who believe that because two of the three comparisons pass, the triangle must exist. Having established that the two-arc construction fails when arcs do not meet, the circle-intersection visual proof in the following part of section 7.2 becomes well motivated.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: Applying the Triangle Inequality — Construct and Classify

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100; (b) 3, 6, 9; (c) 1, 1, 5; (d) 5, 10, 12.
For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side: (a) 1, 100; (b) 5, 5; (c) 3, 7. Describe all possible third-side values for each case.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154
homework.description: Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.

time_bands.activity: Brief review of the triangle inequality decision rule established when the two-arc construction failed: the largest side must be strictly less than the sum of the remaining two. Students state it in their own words before the application tasks begin.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156 ("Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle?...") individually, writing a one-line justification for each set. Circulate; prompt students to identify the largest side first.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159 ("Check if a triangle exists for...") and then Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159 ("For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side..."). The third-side range task stretches students to express the constraint as an inequality interval.
Pairs share their third-side ranges for Try This Q3. Class consolidates: the third side c must satisfy |a − b| < c < a + b. Record this generalised form on the board for reference.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly treat the triangle inequality as a yes/no filter but struggle with the open interval for the third side; emphasise that both the lower and upper bounds are strict (not achieved). Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154 is assigned for independent reinforcement. Watch for unit confusion in part (a) of Q2, section 7.2 p.154 where km appears alongside mm and cm in adjacent parts.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Why Does the Angle Sum Equal 180°?

textbook_items_in_class.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the third angle (using a parallel-line argument) when two angles are: (a) 36°, 72°; (b) 150°, 15°; (c) 90°, 30°; (d) 75°, 45°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°? If two angles are 70°, what is the third? If all angles are equal, what must each be?
In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Find ∠B and ∠C.

time_bands.activity: Students measure the three angles of two different hand-drawn triangles and record their sums via Math Talk, section 7.3 p.164 ("Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third..."). Pairs share results and the class conjectures that the sum is always 180°.

Present the formal parallel-line proof: draw XY parallel to BC through A, identify alternate angles ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C, and observe that ∠XAB + ∠BAC + ∠YAC forms a straight angle at A, giving ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°. Students annotate a diagram of the proof as it is developed.

Students apply the angle-sum property through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165 ("Find the third angle using a parallel-line argument..."), Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165 ("Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°?..."), and Try This Q3, section 7.3 p.165 ("In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°...").

Revisit the parallel-line proof steps verbally. One student explains why the alternate angles are equal; another explains why the three pieces form a straight angle. Consolidate the formal statement: the angle sum property holds for every triangle.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse co-interior angles with alternate angles in the parallel-line diagram; draw attention to the Z-shape (alternate) versus C-shape (co-interior) each time. The exterior-angle result — exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles — follows naturally from the same diagram and is developed in E-23; point students to Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 as a self-study follow-on.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Constructing Triangles from Sides, Angles, and Existence Conditions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°.
Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side? Find examples where they do not.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163
homework.description: For each given angle (a) 30°; (b) 70°; (c) 54°; (d) 144°, find at least two angles for which a triangle is possible and two for which it is not. Find the third angle in each valid case.

time_bands.activity: Demonstrate the SAS four-step construction on the board: draw the base (included side), construct the given angle at one endpoint, mark the second given side on the angle arm, join the endpoints to close. Students replicate with part (a) of Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161 ("Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle...").

Students complete parts (b) and (c) of Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161 independently. Discuss Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162 ("Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible?...") — students identify that an included angle ≥ 180° makes the construction impossible.

Introduce the ASA method: draw the included side, construct the first angle at one endpoint, construct the second angle at the other endpoint, and mark C at the intersection of the two arms. Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162 ("Construct triangles given two angles and the included side...") parts (a)–(c), noting what happens in (c) when the angles sum to 150°.

Quick discussion from Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162 ("Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side?..."). Students articulate the condition — the two base angles must sum to less than 180° — and connect it to the angle-sum property established through the parallel-line proof.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established through the angle-sum property that angles in a triangle sum to 180°, students should see immediately that two base angles summing to or exceeding 180° leave no room for the third; use this reasoning chain rather than re-demonstrating with parallel lines. Watch for protractor errors when constructing the second angle from the opposite base endpoint — students sometimes measure from the wrong baseline direction.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Exterior Angles and Existence Conditions — Reasoning Deeper

textbook_items_in_class.description: Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship between the exterior angle and the two non-adjacent interior angles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle: (a) 35°, 150°; (b) 70°, 30°; (c) 90°, 85°; (d) 50°, 150°.
Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible? Justify from your construction observations.

time_bands.activity: Work through Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 ("Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°...") step by step: extend side BC to D, note that ∠BCA + ∠ACD = 180° (linear pair), and use the angle-sum property to derive ∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B. Students verify with their own angle values.

Students use the exterior-angle relationship to attempt Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163 ("Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle..."). For each pair they check whether the implied third angle is positive, ensuring the triplet sums to 180°.

Revisit Math Talk, section 7.3 p.161 ("Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible?...") with the exterior-angle theorem now available. Students reason deductively: if the included angle reaches or exceeds 180°, the interior angles cannot be positive and sum to 180°.

Students write a two-sentence deductive argument for why the exterior angle must always be greater than either non-adjacent interior angle. Pairs swap and critique each other's reasoning for logical completeness.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the exterior angle with the adjacent interior angle (its supplement) — reinforce that the exterior angle is formed by extending one side, producing a linear pair with the adjacent interior angle. The deduction that the exterior angle exceeds each non-adjacent interior angle follows directly from the fact that those angles are positive; encourage students to write this in algebraic shorthand (∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B > ∠A and > ∠B) as a compact argument.

textbook_segments.title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles

periods.activity_title: Finding the Foot — Altitudes by Folding and Set Square

textbook_items_in_class.description: Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.
Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?
Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square, for the given triangle (extended base case shown also).

time_bands.activity: Define altitude: the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side. Students sketch rough diagrams of acute, right, and obtuse triangles and mark where they expect the altitude foot to fall — inside the base, at a vertex, or on an extension.

Students carry out Activity, section 7.4 p.168 ("Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex..."). After folding, pairs justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base: the fold brings the two halves of the base into coincidence, so the crease bisects the base segment perpendicularly.

Students discuss Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.168 ("In what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?"), drawing rough diagrams and identifying the right-angled triangle. Then they attempt Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169 ("Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square...") for both the standard and extended-base cases.

Class compares folded creases with set-square constructions and discusses whether both methods produce the same perpendicular segment. Students articulate the definition of altitude in their own words and note the distinction between altitude as a line segment and altitude length as a measurement.

periods.teacher_notes: Students are often surprised that the altitude in an obtuse triangle falls outside the triangle — show the extended-base case from Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169 explicitly. The paper-folding justification works best when students are asked 'why does folding one half of the base onto the other force the crease to be perpendicular?' rather than simply told.

periods.activity_title: Mapping the Triangle Family — Sides, Angles, and Names

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170
homework.description: Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.

time_bands.activity: Present the two-axis classification: by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled). Students create a quick two-row table in their notebooks listing properties for each type and give a sketch example.

Students construct the triangle in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.") and classify it by both side-length and angle criteria. They measure angles to confirm their classification.

Groups attempt Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ("Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle..."). Students record what they find possible and explain why, using the angle-sum property.

Class shares findings from Q4: an equilateral triangle must have all angles equal, so each is 60°, ruling out right-angled and obtuse-angled equilateral triangles. A right-angled or obtuse-angled isosceles triangle is constructible. Capture the completed classification map on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often believe that every pair of classification terms can be combined; Q4 efficiently reveals which combinations the angle-sum property forbids — draw out the reasoning chain explicitly. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170 combines obtuse-angled construction with altitude drawing and is assigned for consolidation; watch that students recognise the obtuse angle at R requires the altitude from T to fall outside the triangle.

periods.activity_title: Special Constructions — Hypotenuse-Only Right Triangles and Spatial Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? (Note: other measurements can take any values.)

Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk (on the surfaces) to the opposite corner. Mark the shortest path on a cardboard box and compare with classmates. (Hint diagram shows unfolded surfaces.)

time_bands.activity: Recall the definition of a right-angled triangle — one interior angle equals 90° — and the note from section 7.5 that in a right-angled triangle one leg is itself an altitude. Students state which leg plays that role.

Students attempt Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements?..."). They try several different right-angled triangles sharing the same hypotenuse and compare their results, discovering that infinitely many non-congruent triangles share the same hypotenuse.

Groups work on Figure it Out, section 7.5 p.172 ("Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk on the surfaces to the opposite corner..."). Each group receives a small cardboard box, unfolds one or more surfaces, marks a candidate path, and compares their result with another group's. Groups explain their reasoning for why unfolding the box converts the surface path to a straight-line path on the flat net.

Groups share which unfolding gave the shortest path. Students connect the result to the triangle inequality reasoning: the straight-line distance across the flat net is the minimum possible surface distance.

periods.teacher_notes: The Try This item on hypotenuse-only construction is genuinely open: students may be surprised that one measurement underdetermines the triangle — use this to consolidate the idea that a triangle needs at least three independent measurements. The Shortest Path in a Box puzzle rewards spatial creativity; resist giving the unfolding strategy immediately and let groups discover it through comparison.

textbook_segments.title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles

periods.activity_title: Altitude, Classification, and the Full Construction Toolkit

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: Does an equilateral triangle exist with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does an equilateral triangle of any sidelength exist? Justify.

time_bands.activity: Students revisit Figure it Out, section 7.2 p.158 ("Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.") as a consolidation of the circle-intersection proof. Groups frame a written step-by-step procedure and read it aloud.

Students work through Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159 ("Does an equilateral triangle exist with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does an equilateral triangle of any sidelength exist? Justify."). The justification uses the triangle inequality: for any positive s, s < s + s, so an equilateral triangle always exists.

Students select any one triangle classification from section 7.5 (equilateral, isosceles, scalene, acute, right, obtuse) and construct a specific example, then construct one altitude of their chosen triangle using the set-square method from section 7.4. They label the altitude, identify its foot, and classify the triangle by both systems.

Students share their constructions with a neighbour, who verifies the altitude is perpendicular to the base and confirms the double classification. The pair records any combination they found impossible to construct and states which property prevents it.

periods.teacher_notes: The open construction task in the final stretch of this unit rewards students who recall the relationship between side classification and angle classification from section 7.5 — prompt them to choose a combination and predict before constructing. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159 on the equilateral triangle is a clean capstone application of the triangle inequality: the argument that s < 2s for any positive s is brief but demands careful expression.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly names the classification of a triangle that has all three sides equal?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Equilateral — a triangle in which all three sides are equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the side-based classification: equilateral means all sides equal, isosceles means two equal, scalene means all different.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused 'all sides different' (scalene) with 'all sides equal'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student knows equilateral involves equality but confuses it with the two-equal-sides definition of isosceles.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has conflated a side-based classification with an angle-based classification, suggesting the two systems are not yet distinguished.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the side-classification table in section 7.5 and read each definition aloud.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give one more example of each of the three side-based types and state the corresponding angle measure for the equilateral case.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
exercise.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

items.prompt: A student claims: 'An equilateral triangle can also be obtuse-angled.' Is this claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because equilateral triangles can have any angle sizes.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because an equilateral triangle must have all angles equal to 60°, which are all acute.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because having equal sides does not restrict the angles.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because equilateral triangles are always right-angled.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No. In an equilateral triangle all three angles must be equal, and since they sum to 180°, each angle equals 60°. A 60° angle is acute, so an equilateral triangle is always acute-angled, never obtuse-angled.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-sum property (∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°) with the constraint that all three angles are equal to find each angle is 60°.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected the equal-sides property to the equal-angles consequence of the angle-sum property.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student believes the two classification systems (by sides and by angles) are completely independent, not recognising that equal sides force equal angles.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused 'always acute' with 'always right-angled', indicating a recall error about what equilateral implies.

inclusivity.support: Have the student write ∠A = ∠B = ∠C and substitute into ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180° to find each angle numerically.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words why no equilateral triangle can be right-angled or obtuse-angled using one sentence.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170
exercise.description: Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

items.prompt: In a right-angled triangle, which part of the triangle serves as one of its altitudes?

options.label: B
options.text: The median from the right-angle vertex

options.label: C
options.text: One of the two legs that form the right angle

options.label: D
options.text: The angle bisector from the right-angle vertex

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One of the two legs that form the right angle. Because the two legs meet at 90°, each leg is perpendicular to the other, so either leg is an altitude to the opposite leg serving as the base.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall that an altitude is the perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side, and in a right-angled triangle the legs are already perpendicular to each other.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses the altitude with the hypotenuse, possibly because the hypotenuse is the longest side.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused the altitude with the median, suggesting the two segment types have not been clearly distinguished.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the altitude with the angle bisector, indicating that 'from a vertex' is associated with several segment types and the perpendicularity condition has not been retained.

inclusivity.support: Let the student sketch a right-angled triangle and mark the 90° angle, then trace each leg to see which side it is perpendicular to.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to name which altitude in a right-angled triangle is also the hypotenuse — and to explain why none is, using the definition of altitude.

exercise.description: Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements?

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: A student says: 'I tried to construct a triangle with sides 2 cm, 5 cm, and 9 cm, but the arcs did not meet.' Explain, using the triangle inequality, why the arcs could not intersect, and state what condition the three lengths fail to satisfy.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The triangle inequality requires that every side be strictly less than the sum of the other two. Here the longest side is 9 cm, and the sum of the other two sides is 2 + 5 = 7 cm. Since 9 > 7, the condition is violated: the arc of radius 9 cm centred at one base endpoint lies entirely beyond the arc of radius 2 cm (or 5 cm) centred at the other, so they cannot intersect and no triangle exists.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the largest side (9 cm) is less than the sum of the other two sides (2 + 5 = 7 cm); since 9 > 7, the triangle inequality is violated.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to try the construction with compass and paper to see concretely that the arcs do not meet, then read the sum 2 + 5 aloud before comparing with 9.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if we replace 9 cm with the value 7 cm exactly, do the arcs meet or just touch? What does 'touching' mean for the triangle?

exercise.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: Using the parallel-line argument from the angle-sum property, explain why the three angles of any triangle must always add up to 180°. You may describe the construction steps in your explanation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Draw line XY through vertex A parallel to side BC. The alternate interior angles give ∠XAB = ∠B (since XY ∥ BC with AB as a transversal) and ∠YAC = ∠C (since XY ∥ BC with AC as a transversal). The three angles ∠XAB, ∠BAC, and ∠YAC together make a straight angle at A, so ∠B + ∠A + ∠C = 180°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw a line through A parallel to BC, identify alternate interior angles with each base angle, and use the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first draw the triangle with the parallel line through A and then mark the three angle pieces at A before writing any argument.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if we changed which vertex we drew the parallel line through, would the argument still work? Outline why.

exercise.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle PQR, side QR is extended to a point S so that ∠PRS is an exterior angle. If ∠P = 48° and ∠Q = 67°, find ∠PRS and explain why the exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ∠PRS = ∠P + ∠Q = 48° + 67° = 115°. The reason: the angle sum property gives ∠P + ∠Q + ∠PRQ = 180°, so ∠PRQ = 65°. Since ∠PRQ and ∠PRS form a linear pair, ∠PRS = 180° − 65° = 115°. Alternatively, substituting, ∠PRS = 180° − ∠PRQ = 180° − (180° − ∠P − ∠Q) = ∠P + ∠Q.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the angle-sum property to find the adjacent interior angle, then apply the linear-pair relationship: exterior angle = 180° − adjacent interior angle = sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to first find ∠PRQ using ∠P + ∠Q + ∠PRQ = 180°, then use the linear pair ∠PRQ + ∠PRS = 180°.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what if ∠P were changed to 58° — how would ∠PRS change, and could the exterior angle ever equal 180°? Explain.

exercise.description: Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship between the exterior angle and the two non-adjacent interior angles.

items.prompt: A student draws base AB = 6 cm, then swings arcs of radius 6 cm from A and from B. The two arcs meet at point C. Without measuring, determine the length of AC and the length of BC, and state what type of triangle ABC is.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: AC = 6 cm and BC = 6 cm, because C lies on the arc centred at A with radius 6 cm (so AC = 6 cm) and also on the arc centred at B with radius 6 cm (so BC = 6 cm). Since AB = AC = BC = 6 cm, triangle ABC is equilateral.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A point on an arc of radius r from centre P is at distance r from P; C lies on both arcs, so both AC and BC equal the common radius 6 cm.

inclusivity.support: Offer a number-line sketch showing A and B 6 cm apart, then ask what the distance from A to any point on the A-arc is, before connecting to the construction.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the two arcs had different radii — say, 6 cm from A and 4 cm from B — what would AC and BC be, and would the triangle still be equilateral?

exercise.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: Determine whether a triangle can be formed with sides 11 cm, 14 cm, and 22 cm. Show your working using the triangle inequality, and if the triangle exists, find the range of valid values for a possible fourth (unknown) side if one of the given sides were replaced by an unknown x, keeping the other two sides as 11 cm and 14 cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Check: 11 + 14 = 25 > 22 ✓, 11 + 22 = 33 > 14 ✓, 14 + 22 = 36 > 11 ✓. All three comparisons pass, so a triangle with sides 11, 14, 22 cm can be formed. For the range of x (third side alongside 11 cm and 14 cm): x must satisfy |14 − 11| < x < 14 + 11, i.e. 3 < x < 25. So x can take any value strictly between 3 and 25.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the triangle inequality to all three side combinations, then express the third-side range as |a − b| < x < a + b for the pair (11, 14).

inclusivity.support: Provide a table with three rows, one per comparison, so the student fills in each inequality check before concluding.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the two fixed sides were 11 cm and 11 cm instead, how does the range for x change, and what does the lower bound tell you about the triangle when x approaches it?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156
exercise.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle XYZ, ∠X = 55° and ∠Y = 72°. Find ∠Z. Then determine whether a triangle exists if instead ∠X = 95° and ∠Y = 88° are the two base angles of an ASA construction (given the included side XY). Explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Part 1: ∠Z = 180° − 55° − 72° = 53°. Part 2: ∠X + ∠Y = 95° + 88° = 183°, which exceeds 180°. When the two base angles sum to or exceed 180°, the arms drawn from the base endpoints are parallel (or diverge), so they never meet on the same side of XY. No triangle exists.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the angle-sum property ∠X + ∠Y + ∠Z = 180° for Part 1; for Part 2, check whether the two given angles leave a positive remainder for the third angle.

inclusivity.support: For Part 2, have the student write ∠Z = 180° − 95° − 88° and evaluate to see a negative result, then connect that to impossibility.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if ∠X + ∠Y = exactly 180°, what happens geometrically to the two angle arms in the ASA construction? What figure (if any) do they form?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
exercise.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.

items.section_title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
items.prompt: A triangle has vertices P, Q, R where ∠Q is obtuse. A student wishes to construct the altitude from vertex P to side QR. Describe the steps to carry out this construction using a ruler and set square, and explain why the foot of the altitude falls outside the segment QR.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Steps: (1) Draw the triangle and extend side QR beyond Q (since ∠Q is obtuse, the perpendicular from P will fall outside QR on the Q-side). (2) Place the ruler along the extended line QR. (3) Set the set square on the ruler with one right-angle edge aligned to the ruler. (4) Slide the set square along the ruler until its vertical edge passes through P. (5) Draw the perpendicular from P to the extended line; the foot H lies on the extension of QR beyond Q. The altitude foot falls outside QR because ∠Q is obtuse: the perpendicular from P meets the line containing QR at a point on the far side of Q from R.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Extend the base beyond the obtuse-angle vertex, align the set square to the extended base, slide until its perpendicular edge meets the opposite vertex, and draw the altitude segment.

inclusivity.support: Let the student use the paper-folding method first to see where the crease (altitude) lands, then replicate with set square and ruler.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: for which vertex of the obtuse triangle does the altitude foot lie inside the opposite side rather than on an extension? Explain why.

exercise.description: Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.

items.section_title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
items.prompt: Three towns A, B, and C form a triangle with AB = 8 km, BC = 15 km, and AC = 17 km. A road is to be built from town A perpendicular to road BC, meeting it at point D. Using the triangle inequality, first confirm that these three distances form a valid triangle, then identify what type of triangle ABC is (by its sides).

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Triangle inequality check: 8 + 15 = 23 > 17 ✓, 8 + 17 = 25 > 15 ✓, 15 + 17 = 32 > 8 ✓. All conditions hold, so a valid triangle exists. By sides: AB = 8 km, BC = 15 km, AC = 17 km are all different, so triangle ABC is scalene. (Note: 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17², revealing it is also right-angled, but the question asks only for side classification.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the triangle inequality to all three pairs of sides, then compare all three side lengths to determine scalene classification.

inclusivity.support: Provide a table listing the three pairs and ask the student to compute and record each sum before comparing with the third side.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to compute AB² + BC² and compare with AC² — what additional classification does this reveal, and how does it relate to the altitude from A to BC?

exercise.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.
